Q: Swap 2 lines in text file with assembler A: 
mov ax, currentLine
cmp ax, line1
je swap_with_line2
cmp ax, line2
je swap_with_line1

Once you read line1 you will go and swap it with line2 that you read locally in the swap_with_line2 routine. Therefore the cmp ax, line2 je swap_with_line1 need not exist, nor the swap_with_line1 routine.

But that local read of line 2 must be accounted for through an extra increment of currentLine.

rep movsb
call ReadLine
call WriteLine

Don't you need a lea si, buf right before this call WriteLine, similar to lea si, tempBuf call WriteLine ?

If you program ReadLine so that it accepts an address to load the line to, then the simple solution will not need to copy at all:

copy_and_swap:
    lea  si, buf
    call ReadLine
    jc   eof
    mov  ax, currentLine
    cmp  ax, line1
    je   swap_with_line2

    ...

; line1 is in buf
swap_with_line2:
    lea  si, tempBuf
    call ReadLine
    lea  si, tempBuf
    call WriteLine
    inc  currentLine
    lea  si, Buf
    call WriteLine
    inc  currentLine
    jmp near copy_and_swap

Q: Swap 2 lines in text file using assembler A:

[Edited below] "What is a text file?"

From my previous answer:

If you program ReadLine so that it accepts an address to load the line to, then the simple solution will not need to copy at all:

Now that you have included the ReadLine and WriteLine procedures, I can see that you haven't changed them to actually use that SI parameter! That's certainly one reason why you'll not see a change in the text files.

; IN (si)
ReadLine proc
    mov ah, 3Fh
    mov bx, handle
    lea dx, buf           <==== change to   MOV DX, SI
    mov cx, 128
    int 21h
    jc @exit
    cmp ax, 0     
    je @exit
    mov bufLen, ax
    ret
@exit:
    stc
    ret
ReadLine endp

; IN (si)
WriteLine proc
    mov ah, 40h
    mov bx, handle2
    lea dx, buf           <==== change to   MOV DX, SI
    mov cx, bufLen
    int 21h
    ret
WriteLine endp

Tip: first make the program work with hardcoded line numbers:

line1 dw 2
line2 dw 3

Afterwards you can add a separate input for the line number(s), so you can keep it simpler.

What is a text file?

A text file usually is a collection of sentences that are made up of characters and punctuation marks. Every sentence ends with a newline sequence that on the DOS platform is made up of the bytes 13 (carriage return) and 10 (linefeed). The length of a sentence is variable, so there's typically a mixture of short and long sentences.

What your program tries to accomplish and the solution that I have proposed until now, is totally different from the above definition of what a text file is. Your approach is rather to swap two adjacent equal-sized records from a file. It is of course still possible for such records to contain actual text characters and punctuation marks. Possibly there's even padding that was added to obtain a fixed record size like say 128.

  • Your current program is built upon the premise that the two lines are adjacent to each other, therefore having the user input two line numbers is kind of silly as the second line number necessarily needs to be line + 1.
  • Your current program also always reads 128 bytes for one line, so more logically I would consider reading anything less than 128 to be a partial record or in case 0 bytes were reported the end of the file. Partial records either constitute an error or else can be regarded as the end of the file too.
  • Your current program forgets to inspect the outcome of the ReadLine proc on the adjacent line. It's easy to see that there can be no swapping if the adjacent line simply doesn't exist.

By now it should be clear that you will have to find out what it truly is that your task is about. This is also really what those several downvotes are saying.

Q: Is there any way in Java (even if "unsafe") to instantiate an uninitialized object directly at a specified address? A:

Is there any way in Java (even if "unsafe") to instantiate an uninitialized object directly at a specified address?

You can't do this in "pure" Java.

You can't do that with Unsafe. Unsafe does allow you to create a Java object without causing any constructor to run1, but you can't specify what address it would be allocated at.

You could in theory do it with native code2 called from JNI3, but it would be a difficult / risky thing to do. If the object is in a heap managed by the Java GC, you would have to do everything in ways that wouldn't crash the GC and/or the allocator. If it is not in the heap, then you have the problem of how to handle references; e.g. to avoid the GC or memory barriers from blowing up when they sees them.

My motivation is to enable really, really fast serialization and (often deep) copying, and to create collections of objects with much better memory locality than typical higgledy-piggledy heap-allocated objects, as part of prototyping a new (fast) JVM language.

OK ... so basically that entails modifying the JVM's memory management mechanisms. It sounds like you need to design and implement a brand new JVM implementation that deals with allocation, etcetera in the way you want it to. Of course, that makes your project larger than you probably envisaged.

This would not be done on (regular) heap memory; but direct ByteBuffer, or off-heap memory allocated through Unsafe, or MemorySegment (from FFM) are all possible candidates

I don't think this changes anything. A Java object that is "allocated" inside any off-heap memory segment (be it a direct ByteBuffer or a MemorySegment or an Unsafe allocation) needs to have a reference; i.e. a memory address. If you assign the memory reference to a local variable or object fields (and possibly other things) then it may be visible to the GC and/or to memory barriers. These will assume that the reference is a valid on-heap object reference, and will (most likely) crash the JVM immediately or lead to further heap corruption. The JVM assumes that all Java object references are on-heap.

1 - This is used by the Java Object Serialization classes.
2 - Or any other supported mechanism for calling native code from Java. The performance of the mechanism is moot ... since at some level you will have to "wear" it if you use a conventional JVM.
3 - You can in theory do anything (permitted by the host OS) in native code.
